description:
You are a plowman's son the day the old royal falconer chooses you from the village line, and by nightfall you are learning to lace a hood over the eyes of the king's own gyrfalcon inside a silent stone mews. Follow one falconer's whole life at a medieval royal court — a triumphant first flight before the king, a single storm that nearly costs you everything, and the quiet, hard-won respect of a servant who once sat only four seats from the throne.

A calm, unhurried second-person story to relax or fall asleep to, built on real medieval falconry training, law and court history, from the hooded mews to the hawk-by-rank hierarchy of the Boke of Seynt Albans.
era_setting: A royal English court in the early 1480s: grey stone keeps and a low stone mews within the bailey wall, muddy village lanes beyond, wool and leather clothing in browns, greens and faded reds, and the hooded gyrfalcons, jesses and bronze bells of the royal hunt.

characters.look: a lean man shown from a barefoot village boy of about twelve to an old man past sixty: sun-browned skin, dark brown hair tied back when grown and grey and cropped short in old age; wears a plain undyed wool tunic as a boy, later a weathered green-brown leather jerkin with a thick leather falconry gauntlet always on one arm, ageing into a deeply lined, calm face

a stooped, elderly falconer with a close-cropped silver-grey beard, deeply weathered face and calm pale eyes, missing the tip of one finger on his gloved hand; wears a plain dark green wool coat, a wide leather belt hung with a hawking bag, and a well-worn leather gauntlet
a broad-shouldered man in his middle years with a short greying beard and steady dark eyes; wears a rich crimson velvet cloak trimmed with grey fur, fine leather boots, and a plain gold circlet

a lean, sharp-featured young knight with pale blond hair, a thin mustache and a permanent thin-lipped expression; wears a fine blue-grey doublet with silver thread embroidery and a jeweled dagger at his belt

shown first as a small fair-haired toddler and later as a slim young man who resembles his father, with lighter brown hair tied back; wears a plain undyed tunic as a child and a green-brown leather jerkin with a gauntlet as a grown falconer

shorts.title: The King's Hawk Vanishes Into the Storm #shorts
shorts.description: A royal falconer risks everything to find the king's lost hawk in a single stormy night. #history #falconry #shorts

scenes.narration: You are the servant boy who flies the king's own hawk, until one storm nearly takes her from you forever.
Thunder cracks, and your gyrfalcon bolts straight into the black clouds chasing a fleeing heron.
You swing the lure until your arm burns, but the wind steals her bells away.
All night you walk the wet fields alone, calling for a bird who has no name.
Near dawn, faint bells ring from a low branch heavy with rain.
She hangs tangled and exhausted in the branches, too proud to call for help.
What happens when you finally reach her decides whether you keep your place at the king's own table.

shorts.title: He Broke the Rules to Sit Near the King #shorts
shorts.description: A plowman's son rises through a medieval court by hand-raising the king's own gyrfalcon. #history #medievalhistory #shorts

scenes.narration: A law says a servant may only fly a kestrel, yet they hand you the king's own gyrfalcon.
Kings fly gyrfalcons, yeomen fly goshawks, servants fly kestrels, your master says, reciting the old ranks like scripture.
You slip her hood before the whole hunting party, and the sky itself seems to hold still.
She climbs until she is only a speck, then falls like something dropped from heaven.
When she returns to your glove, the king laughs aloud in delight.
By nightfall you sit four seats from the king, closer than any servant should.
One jealous courtier is already asking what a plowman's son could possibly deserve.
One storm is coming that will threaten everything you have ever won.

editor_notes: The critic cut an invented place name and a conflated legal fact, moved the sourced 'four seats from the king' detail into the story, and gave the jealous courtier's thread a real resolution instead of dropping it.
